title: What is the difference between smoke testing (a quick "is the build even testable" check of critical paths), sanity testing (a narrow check that a specific fix/area works), and regression testing (re-running a broad suite to confirm existing behavior still works), and where does each run in a CI/CD pipeline (smoke on every build/deploy gate, sanity after a targeted change, regression before release)?
shortTitle: Difference between smoke, sanity, and regression testing and where each runs in CI/CD

s1_definition.profdef: Smoke, sanity, and regression are three testing scopes that differ by breadth and intent. Smoke testing is a shallow but wide check that the most critical paths of a freshly deployed build work at all, so it decides whether the build is even worth testing further. Sanity testing is a narrow, deep check that one specific change or bug fix actually behaves correctly, without re-testing unrelated areas. Regression testing is a broad suite re-run across existing features to confirm that a change did not break previously working behavior. In a CI/CD pipeline, smoke runs as a fast gate on every build and deployment, sanity runs immediately after a targeted change, and the full regression suite runs before a release to production.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India just installed a new version of its online banking system overnight. Before letting customers in, a staff member logs in, checks a balance, and makes one small transfer to confirm the lights are on and the doors open; that quick "is it alive" check is smoke testing. Later a developer fixes only the funds-transfer screen, so a tester checks just that screen thoroughly to confirm the fix works, without re-checking loans and statements; that focused check is sanity testing. Finally, before the bank announces the release to all customers, the whole bank is tested end to end, transfers, loans, statements, cards, to be sure the new change did not silently break anything that used to work; that complete re-check is regression testing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Smoke is a wide-but-shallow "is the build alive" gate on every deploy, sanity is a narrow-but-deep check that one change works, and regression is a broad re-run that confirms old behavior still works before release.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Smoke, sanity, and regression are three testing scopes that differ by breadth and intent. Smoke testing is a shallow but wide check that the most critical paths of a freshly deployed build work at all, so it decides whether the build is even worth testing further. Sanity testing is a narrow, deep check that one specific change or bug fix actually behaves correctly, without re-testing unrelated areas. Regression testing is a broad suite re-run across existing features to confirm that a change did not break previously working behavior. In a CI/CD pipeline, smoke runs as a fast gate on every build and deployment, sanity runs immediately after a targeted change, and the full regression suite runs before a release to production.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India just installed a new version of its online banking system overnight. Before letting customers in, a staff member logs in, checks a balance, and makes one small transfer to confirm the lights are on and the doors open; that quick "is it alive" check is smoke testing. Later a developer fixes only the funds-transfer screen, so a tester checks just that screen thoroughly to confirm the fix works, without re-checking loans and statements; that focused check is sanity testing. Finally, before the bank announces the release to all customers, the whole bank is tested end to end, transfers, loans, statements, cards, to be sure the new change did not silently break anything that used to work; that complete re-check is regression testing.

**One line to remember:** Smoke is a wide-but-shallow "is the build alive" gate on every deploy, sanity is a narrow-but-deep check that one change works, and regression is a broad re-run that confirms old behavior still works before release.

sections.s2_technical:
Smoke testing, sometimes called build verification testing, is the first thing you run against a new build. It touches many critical features but only lightly, confirming that the application starts, the main screens load, authentication works, and the core happy-path flows do not immediately fail. The purpose is a fast reject: if smoke fails, there is no point running the expensive full suite, so you fail the pipeline early and send the build back. Smoke suites are intentionally small and fast, often a handful of tests that run in a minute or two, because they gate every single build and deployment. In code terms you might tag them so the runner can select only them, for example in Playwright you would tag a test with `@smoke` and run `npx playwright test --grep @smoke` so only critical-path checks execute.

Sanity testing is narrow and deep. After a specific bug fix or a small feature change, you do not want to re-run everything; you want to confirm that the changed area now behaves correctly and that its immediate neighbors still make sense. For example, if a developer fixed a rounding bug in interest calculation, a sanity check exercises several interest scenarios in depth, boundary amounts, zero balance, large balance, but does not re-test the card module. Sanity testing is often unscripted or lightly scripted and is a subset chosen by judgement, whereas smoke is a fixed predefined set. The distinction interviewers want is that smoke is breadth-first and shallow across the whole system, while sanity is depth-first and narrow on one change.

Regression testing is the broad safety net. Any change, even a correct one, can have side effects elsewhere, because code is interconnected. Regression re-runs a large suite of previously passing tests across many features to catch those unintended side effects. Because this suite is large and slow, you automate as much of it as possible and run it at the right pipeline stage, typically before a release or nightly, rather than on every commit. In a CI/CD pipeline the placement matters: smoke runs on every build and right after each deployment to an environment as a gate; sanity runs right after a targeted change, often by the developer or in the feature branch pipeline; and the full regression suite runs in the pre-release stage, for example against a staging environment before promoting to production. A senior nuance is that these are scopes, not tools, so the same automation framework can hold all three, and you organize them with tags and pipeline stages. Another nuance is that smoke and sanity are sometimes conflated in casual usage, but the precise difference is breadth versus depth: smoke is wide and shallow to accept or reject the build, sanity is narrow and deep to validate a specific change.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India deploys a new build of its online banking service several times a day. If a build is fundamentally broken, running the full two-hour regression suite on it wastes everyone's time and blocks the pipeline. The bank needs a fast gate that quickly answers "is this build even worth testing?" This is exactly what a smoke suite does: a few critical-path checks that run in under two minutes and fail the pipeline immediately if the build cannot even log in or show a balance.

Problem 2 — A developer fixes only the funds-transfer rounding logic. Re-running every test is wasteful, but shipping the fix untested is risky. The bank needs a focused, deep check of just the transfer area. This is exactly what sanity testing does: narrow but thorough validation of the changed feature.

Problem 3 — Before announcing a release to all customers, the bank must be sure the change did not break loans, statements, or cards. This is exactly regression testing: a broad re-run of previously passing tests.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that models a test runner which can execute three named suites, smoke, sanity, and regression, against a small banking system with login, transfer, loan, and statement features. We define a `BankingSystem` with those operations, a `TestCase` with a name and a scope tag, a `TestRunner` that filters and runs cases by scope and reports pass or fail counts, and a `TestingStrategyDemo` main class that runs smoke first as a gate, then sanity on the transfer change, then the full regression suite, printing where each belongs in the pipeline.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile all sources
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/qa/strategy/*.java

# Run the demo
java -cp out com.bank.qa.strategy.TestingStrategyDemo

# In a real Playwright project you select scopes by tag:
npx playwright test --grep @smoke        # fast deploy gate
npx playwright test --grep @sanity       # after a targeted change
npx playwright test --grep @regression   # before release
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a fresh build of the banking system with login and transfer healthy, and a test catalog containing two smoke, two sanity, and four regression cases.

Step 1: CI stage one runs the smoke scope. The runner filters the catalog to the two cases tagged SMOKE and executes them. The data here is just pass or fail booleans from the system's critical paths.

Step 2: Both smoke checks pass, so the gate opens and the pipeline proceeds. If either had failed, the runner would return false, the demo would log a severe message, and the pipeline would stop here without running anything expensive.

Step 3: CI stage two runs the sanity scope on the transfer change. The runner executes the two SANITY cases in depth, a positive transfer of fifty thousand rupees and a zero-amount transfer that must be rejected. The zero case passes because the system correctly refuses a non-positive amount.

Step 4: CI stage three runs the full regression scope. The runner executes all four REGRESSION cases across login, transfer, loan, and statement, confirming no feature regressed.

Step 5: The runner reports pass counts per scope. The final output shows each stage and whether it passed, mirroring how a real pipeline gates on smoke and only reaches regression before release.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Smoke, sanity, and regression are three testing scopes that differ by breadth and by intent. Smoke testing is a wide but shallow check of the most critical paths of a freshly deployed build; its only job is to answer "is this build even worth testing?" so it runs as a fast gate on every build and deployment and fails the pipeline early if the application cannot even start, log in, or perform a core action. Sanity testing is the opposite shape, narrow but deep; after a specific fix or small change I check just that area thoroughly, without re-testing unrelated features, so it runs right after a targeted change. Regression testing is the broad safety net that re-runs a large suite of previously passing tests across many features to catch unintended side effects, and because it is slow I run it in the pre-release stage, typically against staging before promoting to production, or nightly.

The way I keep these straight is to remember that smoke is breadth-first and shallow to accept or reject the build, sanity is depth-first and narrow to validate one change, and regression is broad to protect existing behavior. They are scopes, not tools, so one automation framework holds all three, and I organize them with tags and pipeline stages rather than separate projects.

At the National Bank of India I built exactly this layering. Our online banking service deployed several times a day, so I tagged a tiny smoke suite of login, balance, and a one-rupee transfer that ran in under two minutes and gated every deployment; if smoke failed we rejected the build immediately instead of wasting an hour on the full suite. When a developer fixed only the interest-rounding logic, I ran a focused sanity pass over several interest scenarios including boundary amounts, without touching cards or loans. Then before each release I ran the complete regression suite against staging, covering transfers, loans, statements, and cards, to be sure the change had not broken anything that previously worked. Being able to explain not just the definitions but exactly where each sits in the pipeline, smoke as the per-deploy gate, sanity after a targeted change, and regression before release, is what shows an interviewer I have actually designed a testing strategy rather than memorized three words.

---

keyPoints: Smoke test: basic check after deployment. Sanity: focused check after fix
Regression: ensure existing features still work after changes
Functional: does it work? Non-functional: performance, security, usability
